desc:
For every window size k from 1 to n, look at all contiguous windows of k consecutive elements of nums and take the minimum of each window. Let ans[k-1] be the largest of those minimums. Return the array ans of length n.

Example: for [10, 20, 30, 50, 10, 70, 30] the answer is [70, 30, 20, 10, 10, 10, 10]. For size 2 the window minimums are 10, 20, 30, 10, 10, 30, whose maximum is 30.
hints: Computing every window minimum for every size is O(n<sup>2</sup>) with a running minimum. Instead of fixing the size, fix the element that is the minimum.
If nums[i] is the smallest element in a stretch of length len (bounded by smaller elements on both sides), then nums[i] is the minimum of some window of every size from 1 up to len.

Compute len for each i with a monotonic stack and record ans[len-1] = max(ans[len-1], nums[i]). Then sweep from large sizes to small ones doing ans[k] = max(ans[k], ans[k+1]), since a window of size k+1 contains a window of size k with a minimum at least as big.
editorial: For an index i let L and R be the nearest strictly smaller elements on each side (or the borders). The stretch L+1..R-1 has length len = R - L - 1 and nums[i] is its minimum. A window of size exactly len placed on that stretch has minimum nums[i], so ans[len-1] ≥ nums[i]. Shorter windows inside the stretch that still contain i also have minimum nums[i], which is handled by the sweep below.

The answer is non-increasing in the window size: any window of size k+1 contains a window of size k whose minimum is at least as large. After placing every nums[i] at ans[len-1], a backward pass ans[k] = max(ans[k], ans[k+1]) propagates the values to smaller sizes. Size n always has an entry because the global minimum owns a stretch of length n. The stacks give all stretch lengths in O(n), so the whole algorithm is O(n).
